props.title: Back to School
props.initialSlug: Self-made millionaire crashes son's college experience

sections.content: **Back to School** (1986) represents peak Rodney Dangerfield, unleashing his rapid-fire one-liners and self-deprecating humor in the perfect setting - a college campus where his wealthy businessman character enrolls alongside his son. The film brilliantly satirizes academia while celebrating education, following similar DNA to **Animal House** (1978) but with a fresh twist on the college comedy formula. Director Alan Metter captures the excessive wealth and materialism of the 1980s through Dangerfield's character Thornton Melon, who literally buys his way into college and tries to buy success - until he learns genuine achievement requires real effort.

sections.content: The film excels by pairing Dangerfield's working-class millionaire character with intellectual elites, creating perfect comedic friction. This clash of worlds echoes through later films like **Billy Madison** (1995) and **Accepted** (2006), where outsiders similarly infiltrate educational institutions. The movie's greatest strength is how it balances broad comedy with genuine heart - Thornton's relationship with his son Jason provides emotional stakes that ground the zaniness.

**Back to School** also features an incredible supporting cast including Sally Kellerman, Burt Young, and a young Robert Downey Jr. Most memorably, author Kurt Vonnegut appears as himself in a brilliant meta-joke where Thornton hires him to write a paper about his own books. This scene inspired similar academic satire in films like **Wonder Boys** (2000) and **The Paper Chase** (1973). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Campus Comedy

sections.content: While **Back to School** followed the success of **Animal House**, it helped establish new tropes for campus comedies that would influence films for decades. Its "fish out of water" premise and emphasis on second chances inspired everything from **Legally Blonde** (2001) to **22 Jump Street** (2014). The film's commentary on privilege and bought influence in higher education remains remarkably relevant, predating similar themes in documentaries like **Operation Varsity Blues** (2021).
